name: Gourmanchéma
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Chantoux, A., A. Gontier & A. Prost. 1968. Grammaire gourmantche. Dakar: IFAN. (full grammar; PHOIBLE inventory AA 727 marks Gulmancema as tonal but gives no stress statement)

new_statements.quote: Phonemic tones are very high /"/, high /'/, mid /-/, low /`/ and rising glide /ˇ/. Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs. Length is phonemic for each vowel and is indicated by writing the vowel twice. [p. 32] ... Only three tones, very high /"/, high /'/ and mid /-/ occur with the simple nouns. Stress, which always occurs on the base, is not marked. [p. 55]
new_statements.citation: Beckett, Eleanor. 1974. A linguistic analysis of Gurma. MA thesis, University of British Columbia (Department of Linguistics). viii+151 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 (Phonology), p. 32 (PDF page 42), immediately below Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes'; reinforced p. 55 (PDF page 65) in the section on noun tonal patterns
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (161 pp., ABBYY text layer; extracted text read, no scanned needed) is Eleanor Beckett, A Linguistic Analysis of Gurma, MA thesis, UBC, April 1974. Quotes verified at the stated locators: thesis p.32 = PDF p.42, directly under Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes': 'Phonemic tones are very high /"/, high /'/, mid /-/, low /`/ and rising glide /ˇ/. Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs. Length is phonemic for each vowel and is indicated by writing the vowel twice.' (verbatim; only the scanned rendering of the low and rising-glide diacritics is garbled). Thesis p.55 = PDF p.65, section 'The noun tonal patterns': 'Only three tones, very high /"/, high…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gurma is a tone language (very high, high, mid, low + rising glide) that also has non-contrastive, predictable stress: in nouns stress falls on the 'base' syllable (the lexical root that sits between the noun-class prefix and the class suffix, e.g. o-BA-do 'chief'), and in verbs on the first syllable (verbs lack a class prefix, so this is again the root-initial syllable). Stress conditions vowel allophony (short/very short vowels in unstressed syllables, pp. 36-37) and is not marked in Beckett's transcriptions because it is fully predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for the modern language. In Appendix 2 (pp. 148-149) Beckett reinterprets Koelle's 1854 notation: 'Koelle's length sign really indicates primary stress while his accent indicates secondary stress', and notes Koelle generally marked stress 'on the base of the Gurma words where it falls today', occasionally on the prefix.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress; the only variability noted is Koelle's occasional prefix-stressed 19th-century records, attributed to speaker syllabification (p. 148).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (noun = prefix + base + suffix; verb stem). Source is a 1974 MA thesis on the Fada N'Gurma dialect, based on the author's fieldwork; tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody. Confidence medium because the statement is brief and no later instrumental or specialist (Rialland, Naba) confirmation was accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Beckett 1974 describes the Fada N'Gurma dialect (Burkina Faso), the central/standard variety of Gourmanchéma [gour1243]; no separate glottocode for the dialect. Tersis 1967 (unopened) describes the Kpana variety in northern Togo.

sources.locator: Chapter 2 (Phonology), p. 32 (PDF page 42), immediately below Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes'; reinforced p. 55 (PDF page 65) in the section on noun tonal patterns
sources.note: Ch. 2 phonemics, p.32: 'Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs.' p.55: 'Stress, which always occurs on the base, is not marked.' p.14: stress marked with a preceding [ˈ] before the stressed syllable; stressed vs unstressed syllables condition vowel allophones (pp.36-37). Appendix 2 (pp.148-149) reads Koelle's 1854 length sign as primary and his 'accent' as secondary stress. Language is tonal (very high/high/mid/low + rising glide).
